case_study_insert.main_stem: Greywater Slate Quarry (GSQ) is a private limited company in the primary extraction and construction-materials sector, quarrying and dressing roofing slate for builders, roofers and heritage restoration contractors. Founded in 2013 by Mared Llewelyn, it employs a workforce of 46 and operates a flat organisational structure with democratic leadership. GSQ plans to invest $700,000 in a diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line to cut waste and lift output, financed by a $450,000 ten-year bank loan and $250,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $225,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.10 a unit and a selling price of $9.60, and currently produces 75,000 units a year. Its cutting-section defect rate has reached 6.3%, sending valuable slate to low-value aggregate.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — September 2025: The quarry dressed and graded 18,750 units of roofing slate last quarter, with 6.3% of pieces rejected for cracks or thickness faults, up from 4.4% a year ago. Average order fulfilment is 4 days. Market research of 350 roofing contractors and architects found that 57% would pay a 6% premium for certified matched-size slate, and 68% rank guaranteed monthly deliveries as decisive. A safety audit recorded 2 wire-saw near-misses; guarding retrofit quotations total $28,000. A training review shows 14 of 46 staff lack diamond-wire saw refresher certification; the alternative on-the-job training is available at no fee, while off-the-job training courses at the local college cost $780 per employee.

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, its second rise this year, increasing costs for variable-rate borrowers. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 5.5% to $12.10 per hour from April 2026, lifting payroll costs for labour-intensive dressing crews. (3) Diesel, blasting and haulage costs for quarry operators rose 8.6% year-on-year, construction-input inflation stands at 6.0%, and government public-building repair spending grew 3.8%.

questions.question_text: GSQ plans to finance part of its diamond-wire sawing and computerised sorting line with a ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for GSQ of using retained profit to fund the expansion instead of the bank loan.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit costs GSQ no interest or arrangement fees, protecting cash at a time when fixed costs already run at $225,000 a year. The central bank has raised its base rate from 4.5% to 5.0%, so every variable-rate dollar borrowed becomes more expensive; funding $250,000 internally avoids that exposure, preserves the $5.10 variable-cost cushion on 75,000 units, and avoids weakening the $9.60 selling price that roofers and heritage contractors currently accept for certified matched-size slate. Every dollar not paid as interest can absorb the 8.6% rise in diesel, blasting and haulage costs without cutting the 57% of contractors who would pay a 6% premium.

Point 2: Retained profit keeps full ownership and control with Mared Llewelyn and the existing shareholders. No lender can impose covenants on how the sawing line is operated, on staffing levels across the flat democratic structure, or on future investment; GSQ can time installation around the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending. It also avoids collateral risk against the $700,000 plant itself, which could be repossessed under the bank loan if 6.3% defect rates persisted and heritage orders slipped past the expected monthly delivery guarantee.

Quality of finance: Using $250,000 retained profit for part of the $700,000 line means the bank loan covers only $450,000, keeping repayments well inside the cash flow generated at the current 75,000 units of output and matched against the premium-pricing upside identified in the market research.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Greywater Slate Quarry and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: GSQ is marketing its certified matched-size roofing slate to roofers and heritage contractors. Consider architectural magazine print advertising, roofing-trade exhibitions, or targeted email marketing to contractors. Which should GSQ choose to promote the slate? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Architectural magazine print advertising: Advertising in the magazines read by architects and heritage specifiers gives GSQ credible exposure to the people who write slate into restoration and new-build specifications. Print suits a high-value, durable product: colour photography of the new sawing line, certified matched-size slate and its chain-of-custody paperwork can be shown in detail, and the 57% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 6% premium for matched-size slate are precisely the type to notice certificates. Drawbacks: response is slow, readership among younger specifiers is falling, and GSQ cannot easily prove who enquired after the advertisement appeared.

Roofing-trade exhibitions: Exhibiting at roofing and heritage shows puts GSQ face-to-face with the 350 roofing contractors and architects surveyed, lets buyers handle matched-size samples, and builds relationships where the 68% who rank guaranteed monthly deliveries as decisive can be reassured about the new computerised sorting line. However, stands, travel and sample freight are expensive, there are only a few shows a year, and most visitors are unrelated or browsing — cost per qualified lead is high for a 46-employee private company financing a $450,000 bank loan.

Targeted email marketing: A direct email campaign to the 350-contractor and architect mailbox lists costs little, can carry data sheets, delivery calendars and the matched-size certification, and produces measurable open, reply and quote-request rates tied to the 4 days order fulfilment promise. It demands clean data and regular, readable content, risks being ignored as spam, and cannot replace the tactile proof of slate samples.

Recommendation: GSQ should choose targeted email marketing, supported by sample-box mailings to the highest-value heritage specifiers identified in the research. It is the cheapest option per qualified lead, directly reaches the exact buyers identified in its market research, is measurable in a way print is not, and fits a 46-employee quarrier financing a bank-loan expansion better than the high-cost, infrequent exhibition circuit. Magazine print advertising is rejected as slow, falling in reach and impossible to tie to quote requests; roofing-trade exhibitions are rejected as too costly and too episodic to sustain order momentum. Email alone also cannot close large heritage contracts, so GSQ should reserve a small exhibition budget only for one flagship show per year.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of GSQ with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of GSQ with a well-justified recommendation explaining why magazine print advertising and exhibitions are rejected.

questions.question_text: GSQ's cutting-section defect rate has reached 6.3%. Explain two benefits for GSQ of using democratic leadership to motivate its quarry and dressing crews.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership gives GSQ's 46 quarry workers a genuine voice in setting sawing-shift patterns, safety rotas around the diamond-wire cutters and rest-break scheduling for dusty dressing bays. Being involved in decisions satisfies their esteem and social needs (Maslow) and gives them ownership of the quality of the 18,750 units dressed last quarter. Workers who help shape the rules are far more likely to flag thickness and crack faults early, attacking the 6.3% defect rate before slate reaches low-value aggregate, cutting waste on a product line where every fault destroys a resaleable $9.60 unit.

Point 2: Involving staff in safety and quality decisions produces practical ideas the flat structure can adopt within days — for example, suggestions that cut the 2 wire-saw near-misses recorded in the audit or that speed matched-size grading checks. Higher commitment from involvement improves concentration on the grading tables, lifts output consistency toward the 75,000 units a year needed to service the $450,000 bank loan, lowers accident risk for the 46-strong workforce, and makes retention easier — directly countering the difficulty of hiring specialist dressing labour in a remote quarrying location.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GSQ's defect rate, safety and output.

questions.question_text: Fourteen of GSQ's 46 staff lack diamond-wire saw refresher certification. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at $780 per employee. Which should GSQ choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Training 14 staff at the quarry keeps them productive while they learn GSQ's own diamond-wire saws, tension settings and thickness tolerances, costs nothing in course fees, and protects the 18,750 units dressed last quarter. Experienced sawyers show trainees the exact faults that cause 6.3% rejects, so skills transfer is immediate and machine-specific. Drawbacks: supervising sawyers lose output time, bad habits can spread from operator to operator, and there is no external certificate for insurers or the 350-contractor customer base — a real gap while GSQ is bidding for heritage contracts that increasingly demand audited safety records after the 2 wire-saw near-misses.

Off-the-job training: The college course at $780 per employee gives structured, accredited refresher certification covering blade geometry, tensioning, guarding and emergency stops, costing $10,920 for all 14 staff — affordable against the $700,000 sawing-line investment. It removes staff from bad habits and provides the certificate GSQ's insurers and heritage clients want; however, it takes 14 people off production, the generic syllabus may not match GSQ's specific grading gauges, and travel plus backfill cover adds hidden cost during the busiest dispatch weeks.

Decision: GSQ should choose on-the-job training, supplemented by one external safety audit day for the whole saw crew. On-the-job training costs nothing in fees, keeps dressing output stable while the new sorting line beds in, and passes on machine-specific fault detection faster than a generic college syllabus; the single external audit day satisfies insurers without the $10,920 fee. Full off-the-job training is rejected because pulling 14 of 46 staff off the wire saws for a college week during peak heritage-order season would jeopardise the 68% of customers who rank guaranteed monthly deliveries as decisive, and the certificate alone does not fix the thickness faults causing the 6.3% reject rate — those are corrected at the machine, not in a classroom.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to GSQ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of GSQ.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of GSQ with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption, certification and machine relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how GSQ's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $225,000 ÷ ($9.60 − $5.10) = $225,000 ÷ $4.50 = 50,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 50,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.60 − $5.10 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways GSQ's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. GSQ's managers can compare the 50,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 75,000 units to confirm the quarry operates with a comfortable margin of safety of 25,000 units before the new computerised sorting line adds capacity and fixed costs rise.
2. Contribution per unit of $4.50 lets managers model price moves, for example charging the 6% premium the 57% of surveyed contractors support would lift contribution to $5.08, letting them judge whether the heritage segment will carry the $700,000 investment.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $225,000 and contribution per unit lets managers test whether the slate division can service the $450,000 bank loan, by checking how many extra 36-pallet heritage orders are needed each month to cover the repayments.
4. Unit cost data ($225,000 ÷ 75,000 units + $5.10 = $8.10 a unit) lets managers benchmark each quarter, attack the 6.3% cutting-section defect rate that turns premium slate into low-value aggregate, and renegotiate the $5.10 variable cost with diesel and explosives suppliers amid the 8.6% input-cost rise.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 50,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: margin of safety of 25,000 units at 75,000 units output; 6% premium-pricing modelling; $450,000 loan-service feasibility for the $700,000 sawing line; and unit-cost benchmarking at $8.10 to attack the 6.3% defect rate and input-cost inflation.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate GSQ's financial position by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has GSQ's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: Revenue rose from $5,100,000 to $5,700,000 while cost of sales grew only from $3,060,000 to $3,135,000, so the surplus on trading widened to $2,040,000 and then $2,565,000. Operating profit moved from $765,000 on sales of $5,100,000 to $1,026,000 on sales of $5,700,000. Capital employed grew from $4,250,000 to $5,130,000 as the sawing line and new equipment were funded, and interest payable rose from $225,000 to $255,000.

Evaluation: Performance has strengthened across every measure. The share of revenue kept after production costs widened from 40.0% to 45.0%, driven by the shift toward certified matched-size slate commanding a 6% premium and by the computer sorting line cutting the 6.3% defect rate that previously forced valuable slate into aggregate. The surplus after operating costs improved from $765,000 to $1,026,000, and the return earned on the enlarged capital base rose from 18.0% to 20.0%, meaning the new plant is already earning more than its financing cost. Caution is warranted: capital employed grew faster than the surplus in cash terms, the 6.3% defect rate still destroys margin, and interest payable rose to $255,000 alongside the $450,000 loan, so headroom is thinner than the percentage-point trend suggests.

Conclusion: GSQ's financial position has improved. Both trading margins and the return on the capital base moved favourably, and the improvement is rooted in genuine operating gains from premium, lower-waste production rather than accounting effects. The board should protect the matched-size strategy, close down the 6.3% defect rate before the heritage order book expands further, and watch interest costs as the $450,000 loan amortises.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements and a justified conclusion on whether GSQ's financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for GSQ of introducing a reclaimed-slate takeback scheme with its heritage customers.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: A takeback scheme lets GSQ collect reusable slate off restoration sites, grade and redress it, and resell matched-size reclaimed pieces to the 57% of surveyed contractors willing to pay a 6% premium. It strengthens GSQ's environmental credibility with heritage bodies, cuts demand for newly quarried material and the associated blasting and haulage costs, and deepens switching barriers: contractors who return pallets through GSQ rather than rivals receive priority on guaranteed monthly deliveries, protecting the order book that justifies the $700,000 sawing-line investment.

Disadvantage: Returned slate arrives mixed with lime mortar, nails and battens, so grading and dressing reclaimed pieces consumes scarce skilled labour and warehouse space, and contaminated batches may be unsaleable — worsening the waste position that already sends 6.3% of current production to low-value aggregate. Handling and re-certifying reclaimed matched-size pieces also adds quality-assurance cost and could delay dispatch of new orders, jeopardising the 4 days fulfilment promise valued by the 68% of contractors who rank delivery reliability as decisive.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to GSQ's research data, costs and heritage order book.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 5.0%, the 5.5% minimum wage increase and the 8.6% rise in diesel, blasting and haulage costs will affect GSQ. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.0%): If GSQ's $450,000 ten-year bank loan is variable-rate, a 0.5 percentage-point rise adds about $2,250 a year of interest — modest against fixed costs of $225,000 — though it also discourages new construction borrowing and could slow the 3.8% growth in public-building repair spending that drives roofing-slate demand. GSQ can shield itself by fixing the loan rate; the direct cash impact is small and containable.

Minimum wage increase (5.5% to $12.10): Quarry dressing is labour-intensive. If around 30 of GSQ's 46 staff earn near the current minimum, the 5.5% rise adds roughly $39,900 a year (30 × $11.47 × 2,000 hours × 5.5% ≈ $37,850, plus supervisory knock-ons), on top of fixed costs and with no equivalent productivity gain guaranteed. Democratic leadership and the new sorting line should absorb part of this through fewer rejections and rehandling, but the cash hit is material.

Input-cost inflation (8.6% diesel, blasting and haulage): Fuel, explosives and haulage sit inside the $5.10 variable cost of every unit GSQ produces. Even if they represent about 45% of that cost (≈ $2.30), an 8.6% rise adds about $0.20 per unit, or roughly $14,900 a year on 75,000 units, compounding with the 6.3% defect rate that already forces expensive reprocessing.

Conclusion: The 5.5% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. Unlike the interest-rate rise (about $2,250 a year and fixable through the loan terms) and the fuel increase (roughly $14,900 a year, partly recoverable through the 6% matched-size premium), the wage bill lands directly on GSQ's core dressing workforce — its scarcest resource — adding nearly $38,000–$40,000 a year before any productivity offset, and squeezing the $5.10 variable-cost cushion from day one. GSQ must raise dressing-crew productivity through the new sorting line, renegotiate merchant price lists to pass on part of the increase, and prioritise hiring retentions over expansion until the margin recovers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to GSQ.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on GSQ's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of GSQ with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
